title: The shape of a Pringle
hook: Every Pringle is a precise mathematical saddle called a hyperbolic paraboloid.
peek: A Pringle curves up one way and down the other. That saddle, which mathematicians call a hyperbolic paraboloid, makes the crisps strong, lets them stack in a tube, and gave their engineers some unusual problems on the production line.
lede: Most crisps are random curls of fried potato. A Pringle is the same shape every time: a saddle that bends up along one direction and down along the other. Mathematicians call it a hyperbolic paraboloid. Procter and Gamble launched Pringles in the United States in 1968, and the shape was chosen so that identical crisps could nest neatly inside a tube.

bullets.text: The saddle shape is stiffer than a flat disc of the same thickness, because bending it one way is resisted by its curve the other way. That helps the crisps survive packing and shipping with fewer breakages.

Procter and Gamble chemist Fredric Baur is credited with the stacking idea and the tall can. Because every crisp is identical, they can sit one inside the next without air gaps, unlike crisps tumbled into a bag.
Pringles are not slices of potato. They are pressed from a dough of dried potato flakes, wheat starch and other ingredients, then cut and cooked in moulds that give every one the same curve.
Procter and Gamble has said it used computer simulations of airflow to keep the light, curved crisps from lifting off as they sped along the line. A saddle catches air rather like a small wing.
In 2009 a UK appeals court ruled that Pringles are taxed like potato crisps, even though potato makes up less than half of them. The company had argued they were a different kind of snack.
